overview: Paraguay became independent in 1811, before the map’s 1815 beginning. Wars and dictatorship profoundly affected its people, while household crafts, Guaraní language traditions and shared drinks remained part of social life.

periods.title: Independence and devastating war
periods.summary: Independence preceded the 1864 to 1870 war against Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay.

periods.title: Reconstruction and later conflict
periods.summary: The state continued; the Chaco War against Bolivia took place in 1932 to 1935.

periods.title: Stroessner dictatorship
periods.summary: Police archives document repression under the dictatorship.

periods.title: Transition and constitutional change
periods.summary: The dictatorship ended; the 1992 constitution recognized Spanish and Guaraní as official languages.

sections.title: A house, its objects and public memory

items.text: The Casa de la Independencia in Asunción was built in 1772 and hosted meetings connected with the 1811 independence movement. Its rooms surround a courtyard. A domestic building became a political meeting place before it became a museum in 1965.

The museum identifies a desk-chest as belonging to Fernando de la Mora. Furniture joins weapons and official documents in the collection. Political history also passed through rooms where people sat, stored papers and worked.

An eighteenth-century bed appears in the museum’s bedroom display. It brings private routines into a story often told through public ceremonies. A curated interior helps visitors imagine domestic space, but should not be mistaken for an untouched room occupied continuously since independence.

The Archives of Terror preserve official records of policing and persecution under Alfredo Stroessner. Found in 1992, they supplied evidence for investigating human-rights abuses. Records created to control people can later be used to expose that control.

The archive also documents cooperation between South American dictatorships through Operation Condor. Paraguay’s history of repression therefore crosses national borders. Preserving the records helps account for people harmed by state institutions rather than allowing their experiences to disappear.

The objects of tereré include a jug or thermos, a vessel holding yerba mate and a metal or cane drinking straw called a bombilla. The cold drink makes a familiar set of tools part of everyday sociability.

Pohã ñana herbal knowledge passes through families alongside tereré practices. People associate herbs with healing in this tradition. That cultural association is evidence about beliefs and learning, not proof that every preparation safely treats illness.

Preparing and drinking tereré provides time for conversation and friendship. UNESCO’s account emphasizes a practice shared by diverse participants. A drink can organize a social occasion as effectively as an invitation announcing a formal meeting.

Piribebuy’s Poncho Para’í de 60 Listas has a body, bands and an edging made through different craft processes. Weavers specialize and cooperate to assemble the garment. The result depends on teamwork as well as individual skill.

The craft uses cotton threads and handmade equipment, including wooden tools and seats. Materials and tools are part of the knowledge, not merely background supplies. A finished poncho conceals many small decisions about how to make it.

Poncho techniques have passed from mothers to daughters through demonstration and practice. A safeguarding school adds another route for transmission. The 2023 UNESCO listing records a tradition requiring support, not a craft whose continuation can be taken for granted.

“El Paraguay es un país pluricultural y bilingüe” means “Paraguay is a multicultural and bilingual country.” It is Article 140 of the 1992 constitution. The article names Spanish and Guaraní as official languages and also recognizes other Indigenous and minority languages as cultural heritage.

ending.text: Paraguay survived the nineteenth-century war and continues as a state. Stroessner’s dictatorship ended in 1989, and a new constitution followed in 1992. These political transitions did not erase its communities or make Guaraní cultural life a thing of the past.
